A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of Omni-ID, with matching core equations, methods, and experiments. v1 ends after the references despite appendix cross-references; v2 includes Appendices A–B. Appendix additions therefore mean newly supplied evidence or documentation, without establishing that those experiments were newly performed.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original controllable face-generation and personalized-generation experiments, including quantitative comparisons and ablations in Tables 1–3.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and supplies additional WebFace evaluation, personalized-generation results in Table I, and qualitative comparisons in the appendix.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the fixed-query encoder, few-to-many reconstruction procedure, masked transformer decoder, flow-matching decoder, and both training objectives. Appendix A expands implementation documentation without establishing a revision to the proposed algorithm.

E1.justification: v2 adds filtered WebFace21M identities as a controllable-generation test set; v1 used WebFace21M as alternative pretraining data in an ablation. The two downstream tasks, MFHQ coverage, and licensed personalized-generation training data remain. Additional generator backbones extend model settings rather than task coverage.

E2.justification: The supplied personalized-generation comparisons expand substantially beyond v1's displayed CLIP comparison. Table I evaluates IPA-FaceID, IPA-FaceIDPlusV2, IPA-Full, and PuLID; Figure IV also evaluates IPA-Plus and displays InstantID and PhotoMakerV2 comparisons previously only alluded to in v1. Table 1 retains the same controllable-generation comparators.

E3.justification: v2 extends MFHQ testing to seven inputs, specifies WebFace selection conditions, and supplies FLUX Schnell and SD1.5 evaluation settings. Section 4.1 changes MTD training from 250K to 200K steps and replaces the explicit ArcFace evaluation-feature description with features citing facenet-pytorch. However, Appendix A.2 reports 250K MTD and 5K flow-matching steps, conflicting with v2's main-text 200K and 10K. These are reported setting differences; actual reruns and exact budgets remain unresolved.

E4.justification: Tables 2–3, the pretraining-duration analysis in Figure 9, and the attention visualization are retained. Appendix A adds qualitative findings about token counts, feature aggregation, and injection locations. Appendix B adds template-driven examples and demonstrates transfer of the FLUX-dev-trained representation to Schnell and SD1.5.

E5.justification: Table I newly reports means and standard deviations across identities for personalized generation. v1 provides no corresponding uncertainty reporting. These describe variation across identities, not repeated training runs; neither PDF establishes additional runs or seed-based uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds seven-input MFHQ results, WebFace results, and quantitative personalized-generation comparisons. Examples include Omni-ID's seven-input MFHQ similarity of 0.742 and Table I's 0.8026 ± 0.0421 versus PuLID's 0.7289 ± 0.0572. Previously reported MFHQ entries and Tables 2–3 retain their numbers. WebFace has five values under four input-count labels, preventing reliable assignment of each value to an input count. These additions do not establish same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation and Equations 1–7 remain unchanged. The added Information Bottleneck reference supplies conceptual motivation, without introducing a formal assumption, derivation, theorem, or proof.

C1.justification: Both versions claim a fixed-size holistic identity representation learned through few-to-many reconstruction and complementary decoders, improving identity preservation in two generative tasks. v2's conclusion reiterates input-count scaling and representation structure already claimed in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds specific limitations concerning lighting injection and skin-tone predominance, with proposed remedies involving more diverse data or lighting augmentation. Section 4.2 replaces the claim of better pose accuracy with an interpretation of similar pose errors as evidence of convergence. Section 4.4 also explains the restricted ablation input counts through diminishing returns.

D1.justification: Appendix A supplies extensive previously unavailable details: feature extraction and aggregation, decoder configurations, optimizers, learning rates, batch sizes, GPU hardware, training resolutions, downstream schedules, and initialization. Figure I documents MFHQ filtering and pose-based sampling. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although conflicting training-step counts and main-text versus appendix ArcFace dimensions leave some settings ambiguous.

R1.justification: v2 adds Information Bottleneck literature, additional 3D face-model references, and technical citations including InsightFace, facenet-pytorch, BLIP-2, SDXL, and FLUX-ControlNet. The central positioning against discriminative representations and alongside personalization approaches remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section order and much of the prose are retained. Local revisions condense the introduction and experimental overview, clarify explanations, and revise the conclusion. Appendices A–B organize the newly supplied documentation and supplementary experiments.

P2.justification: The full-page gallery becomes a smaller Figure 8, and the personalized-generation comparison is reduced and relocated as Figure 7. Table 1 becomes a full-width two-dataset display. v2 adds the dataset-construction diagram, expanded qualitative comparison grids, and Table I, substantially changing the visual organization while retaining the main ablation displays.

improvement.justification: v2 supplies quantitative support for the personalized-generation claim that v1 deferred to an absent appendix, adds evaluation beyond MFHQ, and substantially documents training and dataset construction. This makes central claims more assessable and the implementation more transparent. Conflicting training settings, unexplained metric attribution changes, and the WebFace label mismatch remain material reporting flaws, but the gains in available evidence and documentation are substantial overall.
